work.title: Tesla
work.subtitle: Manufacturing controls engineering intern
work.desc: Summer 2026 on a manufacturing controls team in Austin: Siemens PLC and HMI work, and an AI platform that helps engineers debug equipment.
work.summary: A summer on a manufacturing controls team at Tesla in Austin. I split the time between the controls themselves (Siemens PLC and HMI software, interlocks, fail-safe behavior) and the tools around them: an AI engineering platform that reads the team's documentation and helps engineers trace and fix equipment problems. The specifics stay with Tesla; this is the shape of the work.
highlights: Built an AI engineering platform for the controls team: document ingestion, semantic retrieval over manuals and programs, labelled debugging traces, and system graphs of how equipment connects.
Set up versioned evaluations that check AI-generated PLC code against expected equipment behavior and safety constraints before it is used.
Programmed and commissioned Siemens S7-1500 PLC and HMI logic in TIA Portal (SCL, ladder and function block diagram) with process interlocks and fail-safe behavior.
Connected plant systems through REST APIs, single sign-on and RFID.
Troubleshot equipment faults alongside mechanical, electrical and software engineers.

work.title: 4D Mapping
work.subtitle: Object detection and AI optimization
work.desc: A computer-vision workbench I built: put in an ordinary 2D video and it finds the objects, tracks them and rebuilds the scene in 4D, which is x, y and z plus time.
work.summary: A plain 2D video goes in. Object detection finds the subject in every frame, depth models and camera solving lift each frame into 3D, and the frames are joined into one scene you can orbit and scrub through time. Earlier positions stay in the scene as ghosts, so a deer's whole path through the woods shows at once. The demo below comes out of my own pipeline from a single clip, with no 3D scanner and no extra cameras.
highlights: 4D reconstruction from one ordinary video: the camera path solved, the subject tracked frame by frame, and the scene placed in x, y, z and time.
Object detection measured on a 1,000-image hold-out: RF-DETR large finds people at 0.878 AP@0.50 in 35 ms a frame on an M5 Max, against 0.489 for the small on-device model.
Open-vocabulary detection and segmentation (Grounding DINO and SAM) for subjects the stock detectors miss, such as a deer.
Gaussian splats and per-frame 3D Gaussians for the photoreal version of the scene, trained on the real frames and scored on held-out frames.
Fully automatic: drop a clip in a folder and the pipeline runs end to end and writes its own report, with no one in the loop.
Native desktop app in Rust on wgpu with a 4D timeline, orbit, top-down and follow cameras, and manual correction of detections.

work.title: ThinkFree Finance
work.subtitle: Founder and software engineer
work.desc: An AI platform I founded that turns financial news and public records into plain-English explanations, with every number checked against its source.
work.summary: ThinkFree Finance explains markets for people who don't follow them for a living: renters, hourly workers, small-business owners, students. It reads the news, links it to public records and writes plain-English reports. A language model can state a wrong number as confidently as a right one, so the pipeline checks what it can and labels what it can't.
highlights: AI pipeline: news collection, embedding-based clustering, LLM summaries and FAISS retrieval over economic reference texts, built to process over 1,000 articles a day.
Links politicians, bills, lobbying, congressional trades and public spending using SEC EDGAR, OpenFEC, USASpending, BLS, Census and other public sources.
Numbers in generated reports are checked against the source data, and summaries that fail are withheld.
FastAPI website with accounts, MFA, CSRF protection, role-based access and a hash-chained audit log, plus a SwiftUI iPhone app.
Ran my own security review in October 2026 and logged every bug I found with the test that proves the fix.

work.title: hardcaml-pwm
work.subtitle: Digital hardware design in OCaml
work.desc: A rotary-encoder knob that sets a PWM duty cycle, written in Jane Street's Hardcaml. The duty glides to each new value instead of jumping.
work.summary: A small piece of digital hardware written in OCaml with Jane Street's Hardcaml. Turn a rotary encoder and a PWM output follows, sliding to the new duty cycle over a few periods instead of jumping there. Simulated and tested, with the Verilog generated; a learning project that hasn't been run on an FPGA board yet.
highlights: PWM block with interpolation: each new target ramps in over a fixed number of periods and lands exactly, with no rounding error.
Quadrature decoder for an EC11-style encoder: synchronizers, debouncing, direction from the A and B edges, and clicks only on real detents.
Waveform tests in simulation for every block, and generated Verilog.
